title: Predictivism as a Scope Ambiguity: De Re and De Dicto Confirmation of Searched Hypotheses
thesis: When a hypothesis H is selected from a large space for its fit to E, E confirms H (de re) exactly as much as it would have if H had been proposed in advance. What E confirms less is the de dicto proposition 'the output of search S is true'. The Bayesian denial of predictivism and the error-statistical affirmation of it are both correct, about different propositions.
argument_sketch: Distinguish two objects of evaluation: the hypothesis picked out rigidly, and the hypothesis picked out under the description 'whatever S returns on E'. For a coherent agent, P(H|E) is fixed by the prior and likelihood of H and does not depend on how H was found. P(the S-winner is true | E), however, must average over all the hypotheses S could have returned, so it is discounted by the search's reach. I then argue that scientific acceptance, reporting, and policy reliance usually take the de dicto object, because what gets endorsed is the method's verdict. On this reading the physicist's distinction between local and global significance (the look-elsewhere effect) is the same scope distinction. Most canonical predictivist cases have a true de dicto reading and a false de re reading.
why_new: White (2003), Hitchcock and Sober (2004), and Howson and Urbach each locate the predictive advantage in one place: the predictor's reliability, overfitting, or nowhere. None of them notices that the competing verdicts attach to different propositions. Treating the debate as a scope ambiguity explains why both camps' intuitions are stable, and it gives a principled account of when timing-based judgments are apt.

title: Graded Predictivism: Measuring Accommodation in Bits of Leakage
thesis: How far a fit's confirmatory force should be discounted for accommodation is bounded by the mutual information between the data and the choice of hypothesis. 'Prediction' is the special case where that information is zero. Timing matters only as a crude upper bound on this leakage.
argument_sketch: Results in adaptive data analysis (Russo and Zou; Dwork et al.) bound the bias of a data-selected statistic by I(E; choice of H). I adapt these bounds to the evidential setting and show that the excess apparent support of a selected hypothesis over its honest support is controlled by this quantity. The prediction/accommodation dichotomy therefore conceals a continuum. Examples on the continuum include hypotheses chosen after seeing a noisy summary of the data, a coarse histogram, or one variable among many, and each warrants intermediate confirmation. Timing is neither necessary nor sufficient for zero leakage: post-data choices made blind to the data have none, and pre-data choices informed by correlated pilot data have some.
why_new: The philosophical literature treats novelty as binary, whether temporal (Popper, Lakatos), heuristic (Zahar, Worrall), or use-based. The information-theoretic results in computer science have not been brought into confirmation theory. This thesis supplies a quantitative, graded replacement for use-novelty and makes Worrall's criterion a limiting case.

title: The Uniqueness Dividend: When Search Confirms More Than Prediction
thesis: An exhaustive search of a large space that finds exactly one adequately fitting hypothesis confirms that hypothesis more strongly than an equal fit by the same hypothesis proposed in advance and tested alone. The predictivist intuition is reversed whenever the search's negative results are retained as evidence.
argument_sketch: The worry about search conflates two procedures: selecting the best fit, and discovering a unique fit. In the second, the search itself produces eliminative evidence. Every rival in the space is shown to misfit, which raises the posterior of the survivor beyond what its own likelihood ratio provides. A predictor who tests H alone learns nothing about rivals, so the catch-all keeps its prior mass. I show formally that, holding H's fit fixed, the advantage depends on the margin by which rivals fail and on the stopping rule. Stop-at-first-fit searches forfeit the dividend, which explains why they earn suspicion while exhaustive searches (Kepler's orbit-fitting, Mendeleev's alternative arrangements) need not.
why_new: Existing debates presuppose that search can only weaken support. The thesis identifies a mechanism, eliminative information about the rest of the space, through which accommodation by search beats prediction. It also explains the predictivist intuition as an artifact of selection procedures that discard rival-failure information.

title: Capacity, Not Cardinality: Why the Size of a Search Space Is the Wrong Measure
thesis: The number of candidates searched has no direct bearing on how much accommodation should be discounted. What matters is the capacity of the space relative to the data: its ability to fit arbitrary data sets (VC dimension, Rademacher complexity). A search of uncountably many hypotheses can warrant a smaller discount than a search of twenty.
argument_sketch: Fitting a line through 100 points searches a continuum of hypotheses, yet the fit is strongly confirmatory because lines cannot fit most data sets. Choosing among twenty unconstrained post hoc stories can be nearly worthless, because each can be bent to fit anything. Building on statistical learning theory, I argue that the relevant counterfactual is how probable a good fit by some member of the space would have been if the data were noise. That probability is governed by capacity, not cardinality. The resulting principle explains why 'large search' intuitions mislead in both directions. It gives a measure of search that is invariant under redescribing the hypothesis space, which raw counting is not.
why_new: Philosophical discussions of the open question and of multiple comparisons speak loosely of 'large spaces' or 'many hypotheses'. Hitchcock and Sober use AIC, which counts parameters and so also fails in non-parametric and combinatorial spaces. Making capacity the measure resolves the redescription problem for search-based accounts, which otherwise threatens to make the size of the search space arbitrary.

title: Accommodation Confirms Disjunctions, Prediction Confirms Disjuncts
thesis: When a hypothesis wins a large search, most of the confirmation produced by its fit flows to the family it belongs to, roughly the disjunction of near-equivalent winners, rather than to the winner itself. The winner's share is inversely proportional to the effective number of near-fitting candidates.
argument_sketch: In a large space, data that one member fits are typically fitted almost as well by a cluster of neighbours. Conditioning on E then raises the probability of the cluster substantially, but spreads that increase across its members. A hypothesis proposed in advance has no comparably populated neighbourhood in the proposer's credal state, so its incremental confirmation is concentrated. I make this precise and show it explains the cases where accommodating scientists are rightly confident in a framework (a model architecture, a mechanism type) but rightly agnostic about the particular fitted instance. The upshot is that the debate is partly about the grain of the hypothesis under evaluation.
why_new: Lange's (2001) point about arbitrary conjunctions and the overfitting account both address the content of accommodated hypotheses. Neither identifies upward transfer of confirmation to the family as the mechanism. The thesis predicts which level of a theoretical hierarchy accommodation can legitimately support.

title: Predictivism Is About Resilience, Not Probability
thesis: A hypothesis accommodated by search and an identical hypothesis predicted in advance can coherently receive the same posterior probability from the same evidence. They nonetheless differ in resilience (the stability of that probability under further evidence). The predictivist intuition tracks this second-order difference, not a first-order difference in confirmation.
argument_sketch: After a search, the winner sits among many near-rivals whose fit differs only slightly. Small amounts of new data can therefore reshuffle the ranking, and the winner's posterior is fragile even when high. A predicted hypothesis tested against a sparsely populated alternative space has a posterior that later data shift far less. Using Skyrms' resilience and Joyce's evidential weight, I show that standard predictivist cases separate in resilience while potentially agreeing in probability. This explains why scientists who 'believe' the accommodated hypothesis still decline to build on it. Practical acceptance depends on resilience.
why_new: Both sides of the existing debate assume that if there is a predictivist effect it shows up in posterior probability or in a confirmation measure. Relocating it to weight or resilience accommodates the Bayesian invariance results (Howson and Urbach) and the predictivist's data at once, and connects predictivism to the theory of imprecise and weighted credence.

title: Goodhart Predictivism: When Search Optimizes Our Plausibility Cues
thesis: If a search selects hypotheses for fit and also for the features evaluators use as prior-plausibility cues (simplicity, elegance, mechanistic narrative), then neither the fit nor those features retain their evidential value. In that circumstance only genuinely out-of-sample prediction confirms. Here, and essentially only here, timing is irreplaceable.
argument_sketch: Standard search-correction proposals adjust for fit-selection while trusting the evaluator's prior. But the prior is applied through observable proxies, and a search over a rich enough space can optimize those proxies as easily as it optimizes fit. By Goodhart-style reasoning, the correlation between proxy and true prior plausibility collapses among selected hypotheses. A correction for search that uses the proxy-based prior is then itself corrupted. I argue this is the right model for hypotheses generated by large language models and for skilled human storytelling. Data the search could not access is the one evidential channel the search cannot game.
why_new: The literature treats priors as given and search as acting on likelihoods. This thesis identifies a regime where search contaminates the prior. It explains why sophisticated Bayesian corrections for multiplicity can still fail, and delivers a precise, restricted vindication of strong predictivism suited to AI-assisted hypothesis generation.

title: Contamination Is Search: Machine Predictions and the Collapse of the Timing Criterion
thesis: A hypothesis output by a system trained on a corpus that contains, or correlates with, the test data is an accommodation, whenever it was produced. Such cases show that temporal predictivism is not merely imprecise but systematically wrong as a criterion, while search-based accounting gets them right.
argument_sketch: Machine-learning systems routinely 'predict' results that were present in their training data or in data strongly correlated with it, and their outputs precede any human test. Temporal novelty classifies these outputs as predictions. Heuristic novelty is undefined, since there is no intelligible heuristic. Leakage-based search accounting correctly classifies them as accommodations. I generalize this to humans through absorbed 'training data', such as theorists who have unknowingly seen preliminary results or tacit community lore. The upshot is that the evidential category is fixed by the causal-informational path from data to hypothesis, and timing is at best a proxy for the absence of such paths.
why_new: The predictivism debate predates scientific hypotheses generated at scale by trained models. Benchmark contamination is a live methodological problem in AI evaluation. This thesis uses it as a decisive test case between timing-based and search-based accounts, and offers a general account of informational contamination.

title: Derivational Predictivism: Actual History Is Evidentially Irrelevant
thesis: The accommodation discount for a hypothesis should be computed from the smallest search over pre-data information that would have generated it, not from the search that actually produced it. A hypothesis accommodated by a sprawling search that a short principled derivation could have produced in advance is as well confirmed as a prediction.
argument_sketch: Search-based accounts inherit a problem from temporal ones: they make confirmation depend on biographical accidents. Two scientists reach the same hypothesis by searches of very different size, and the evidence apparently supports it differently. I argue the evidentially relevant quantity is counterfactual and agent-neutral: the minimal description length of the hypothesis relative to the pre-data background. This quantity determines the honest prior mass any pre-data reasoner could assign. Actual search history matters only as defeasible evidence of what that minimum is. This vindicates the intuition behind Worrall's heuristic novelty while severing it from the psychology of discovery.
why_new: Worrall's use-novelty and Zahar's heuristic novelty both ultimately depend on the actual construction history, which critics such as Mayo and Hudson have pressed. Replacing actual history with minimal pre-data derivability gives an objective, history-independent version of novelty, a solution neither side has formulated.

title: One Problem, Not Two: Old Evidence and Accommodation via Search-Conditional Likelihoods
thesis: The problem of old evidence and the prediction/accommodation problem share one solution. Old evidence E confirms H to the degree that P(E | H generated by procedure S) exceeds P(E | some output of S fits E). This yields full confirmation for genuinely unsought old evidence and none for evidence used to construct H.
argument_sketch: Counterfactual solutions to the old evidence problem (Howson; Sprenger 2015) ask how probable E would be had it not been known. But they do not say which counterfactual knowledge state is relevant, and this is where accommodation enters. I propose that the right counterfactual holds fixed the generating procedure of H and varies whether E fed into that procedure. Mercury's perihelion confirms general relativity strongly because the procedure that generated general relativity was largely insensitive to it, so the search-conditional likelihood is high. A theory reverse-engineered to fit the perihelion receives no boost. The account unifies the two literatures and removes the arbitrariness from counterfactual-credence solutions.
why_new: The two problems are usually discussed separately (Glymour 1980; Earman; Wenmackers and Romeijn on old evidence; Maher, White, and Barnes on predictivism). Making the generating procedure the index of the counterfactual both fixes the reference point for old-evidence solutions and gives predictivism a principled Bayesian formulation.

title: Timing as a Verification Technology
thesis: For an ideal agent with full knowledge of the search process, timing is evidentially irrelevant. For any community whose members cannot verify one another's search histories, it is not. Pre-commitment is the only publicly checkable upper bound on search, so the debate splits into an ideal question (settled against predictivism) and a social question (settled for it).
argument_sketch: Search-based accounts require a description of the search, but searches are largely private, partly unconscious, and cheaply misreported. A temporal record of a proposal before data access is a costly, timestamped commitment that bounds search for anyone who reads it. Drawing on signalling theory, I argue that in equilibrium unverified claims about small searches carry little information. Communities that treat predictions preferentially are therefore rational even if each individual's ideal confirmation is timing-independent. This explains the preregistration movement without endorsing intrinsic predictivism.
why_new: Preregistration is defended in metascience on practical grounds, and the philosophical debate concerns ideal confirmation. Neither side has argued that the two questions get different answers for a precise structural reason, namely the verifiability asymmetry. The thesis also yields concrete conditions, such as auditable search logs, under which the predictive advantage should vanish.

title: Parallel Prediction Does Not Penalize: Against Field-Wide Multiplicity
thesis: When many independent researchers each propose one hypothesis in advance and the successful one is later singled out, the winner's confirmation is not reduced by the number of competitors. Only searches whose output was sensitive to the very data token in question carry a discount.
argument_sketch: Frequentist multiplicity reasoning implies that a field's collective testing of many hypotheses reduces the significance of any one success. That makes confirmation depend on what strangers did. I argue this conflates the de dicto question about 'the field's best hit' with the de re question about H. Data-sensitive selection lowers H's support relative to its prior. Independent parallel proposals instead leave each proposer's prior intact and merely raise the base rate of successes we hear about. That base-rate effect belongs to a separate source, publication selection of reported data, and should be corrected there. The criterion of data-token sensitivity draws the line precisely.
why_new: Philosophers have not settled what the reference class for multiplicity corrections should be, and the metascience literature tends toward field-wide corrections. The thesis gives a principled criterion, causal sensitivity to the specific data, and separates hypothesis-search effects from file-drawer effects, which are usually lumped together.

title: Generative Priors: Why Searched Hypotheses Need Procedure-Indexed Credences
thesis: An agent whose hypothesis algebra is open and expands as new hypotheses are conceived must set the prior of a newly conceived hypothesis by the reliability profile of the procedure that generated it. When that procedure was a data-guided search, this rationally lowers the prior below what intrinsic plausibility would assign. This is where predictivism lives for bounded Bayesians.
argument_sketch: The Bayesian argument against predictivism assumes a fixed algebra with priors assigned before data. Real agents conceive hypotheses during inquiry, and must assign them priors after the data, drawing mass from a catch-all. I argue the only non-circular basis for that assignment is the frequency with which similar procedures yield true hypotheses. Data-guided search is a procedure whose outputs fit by construction, which makes fit uninformative about truth for that procedure. A coherent open-minded agent therefore assigns accommodated hypotheses smaller priors than predicted ones of equal intrinsic plausibility, and no rule of diachronic coherence is violated.
why_new: Open-minded Bayesianism (Wenmackers and Romeijn) and the problem of unconceived alternatives (Stanford) have not been brought to bear on predictivism. The thesis shows that predictivism follows from the theory of algebra expansion rather than from timing or reliability-of-the-scientist arguments.

title: Predictions Are Searched Too
thesis: Prediction carries its own selection penalty, symmetric to accommodation. Predictors choose which predictions to make, which tests to run, and which successes to publicize, so a predictive success confirms only to the degree that this prediction-side search is accounted for. Once both searches are counted, prediction has no intrinsic advantage.
argument_sketch: Predictivists compare an accommodator who searches over hypotheses with a predictor who is assumed not to search. But prolific forecasters, astrologers, and theorists offering many ad hoc predictions search over future data, and their reported hits are selected. Predictors also choose tests where rivals agree and success is cheap, which is Mayo's low-severity case. I formalize evidential value as a function of the joint search over hypothesis–test pairs and show that standard predictivist examples become symmetric once the predictor's test selection is held fixed. The coin-flip cases of Maher and of Kahn et al. stipulate away predictor-side search, and that stipulation is doing the work.
why_new: The debate has treated prediction as the selection-free baseline. Recognizing search on both sides yields a symmetric principle, explains why prolific predictors earn little credit, and shows that the familiar arguments for predictivism rely on an unacknowledged asymmetric idealization.

title: Accommodation as Double Counting: The Empirical-Bayes Diagnosis
thesis: The illegitimate part of accommodation by search is exactly the double use of data that occurs in empirical Bayes when a hyperparameter (here, the index of the chosen hypothesis) is estimated from the same data it then evaluates. Marginalizing over the index removes it completely, leaving no residual predictive advantage.
argument_sketch: Treat the search space as a hierarchical model whose top-level parameter indexes the candidate. Choosing a candidate by fit then evaluating it on the same data plugs in an estimate of the index, which is the well-understood empirical-Bayes error of using data twice. The fully Bayesian alternative marginalizes over the index, and the resulting posterior on the chosen candidate is invariant to timing. I argue every intuitive predictivist case either involves this plug-in error or involves a prior the accommodator lacks. Neither is a sui generis epistemic feature of timing.
why_new: The 'double counting' charge appears informally in the literature (and in Mayo's critique of Bayesian use of data), but no one has identified it with the precise empirical-Bayes structure. The identification provides an exact correction and a sharp test of whether any predictivist residue survives.

title: Hypothesis Search versus Data Search: An Asymmetry the Debate Has Missed
thesis: For an ideal agent, selecting hypotheses on the data never lowers the support the full data give a hypothesis. Selecting data, subsets, or analyses can, because it changes which evidence is being conditioned on. The 'garden of forking paths' is almost entirely a problem of data search misdescribed as hypothesis search.
argument_sketch: Holding the total evidence fixed, Bayesian support for H is independent of which H was chosen to examine. Choosing which variables, exclusions, and transformations to report, however, changes the conditioning proposition from 'the full data' to 'a selected summary'. The likelihood of the selected summary under H must then incorporate the selection rule. I show that standard p-hacking and forking-paths cases decompose into a hypothesis-search component and a data-search component, and that only the latter makes the evidence weaker, as opposed to the hypothesis less probable a priori. The open question is then answered: large hypothesis searches reduce confirmation only via prior effects, and timing matters only as protection against data search.
why_new: Gelman and Loken and the philosophical discussions of predictivism treat forking paths as a single phenomenon. Splitting it into two components with different epistemic structures shows why the Bayesian 'search is irrelevant' verdict and the methodologist's alarm can both be right.

title: The Logarithmic Ceiling on Predictive Advantage
thesis: The maximum evidential advantage of prediction over accommodation, for a search over a space of effective size N, is about log N bits. Likelihood ratios from accumulating data grow linearly in sample size, so predictivism is a small-data phenomenon. With abundant data the distinction becomes negligible, which explains why it seems decisive in historical cases and irrelevant in mature experimental fields.
argument_sketch: Under uniform or capacity-weighted priors, the cost of locating a hypothesis within a space is bounded by the code length needed to specify it, as in the Occam bounds of learning theory. Once evidence supplies likelihood ratios exceeding this cost, the posterior of the true hypothesis is high regardless of whether it was found by search. I derive the bound and calibrate it against cases: Mendeleev's gallium, the Fresnel white spot, and contemporary genome-wide association studies. The bound predicts when predictivist judgments should matter. It also gives scientists an operational rule: an accommodated hypothesis needs independent evidence of strength at least log N to reach parity with a prediction.
why_new: The predictivism literature is entirely qualitative about magnitude. The thesis supplies a quantitative ceiling, explains the striking historical dependence of the debate's examples on small data, and turns an abstract dispute into a calibrated methodological rule.

title: Erotetic Predictivism: Search Penalties Are Relative to Questions
thesis: Whether and how much a search discounts a fit depends on the question the inquiry was answering, that is, the partition of possibilities under investigation. The same search and data can yield different, equally correct confirmation assessments for different questions. Debates about whether accommodation 'really' confirms less are partly debates about which question is in play.
argument_sketch: A search over N candidates for a mechanism answers the question 'which mechanism?', and its winner bears a multiplicity discount relative to that partition. Relative to the coarser question 'is there any mechanism of this type?', the winner's fit is direct evidence with no discount. Relative to the finer question 'what are the exact parameter values?', the discount is larger. Using the formal theory of questions as partitions, I show that confirmation-by-search is well defined only relative to a partition. Temporal predictivism smuggles in a default question, the one the predictor was asking. This explains why disputes over cases such as Mendeleev's periodic table persist: the parties index to different questions.
why_new: Question-relativity has been developed for explanation and inquiry (van Fraassen; Hintikka; Friedman) but not applied to predictivism. The thesis converts apparently substantive disagreements into identifiable differences of partition and provides a criterion for which question governs acceptance.

title: Effective Search Size: Expert Heuristics as Importance Sampling
thesis: The penalty for search depends on the entropy of the generating distribution over the space (the effective number of candidates the searcher was likely to try), not on the nominal size of the space. A search by a well-calibrated expert can therefore warrant almost no discount, while a naive search of a smaller space warrants a large one.
argument_sketch: No real searcher samples uniformly. Experts try candidates in an order shaped by background knowledge, which is effectively importance sampling from a prior. If that ordering is informative, the fitted winner was likely to be tried early whether or not it fit, and the accommodation discount shrinks to the log of the effective support of the expert's search distribution. I show this explains the asymmetric credit we give to Kepler's search versus that of a crank numerologist. It also implies that the evaluator's assessment of accommodation must partly be an assessment of the searcher's prior, linking predictivism to testimony. The view predicts that the discount should vary with the searcher's track record even when the space is identical.
why_new: Searcher-reliability accounts (White 2003; Barnes 2008) treat reliability as a black box. This thesis gives it formal content as the information-theoretic concentration of the search distribution, and reconciles reliability-based and search-based accounts in one quantity.

title: Convergent Accommodation: When Independent Searches Recover Predictive Force
thesis: If several searchers whose idiosyncratic choices are independent (different spaces, heuristics, or analytic pipelines) independently select the same hypothesis from the same data, their convergence supplies evidence of predictive strength. The strength is roughly that of a prediction whose rivals were each searchers' alternative outputs.
argument_sketch: Accommodation is suspect because the winner may be an artifact of a particular search's idiosyncrasies. Convergence of independent searches is unlikely if the winner is such an artifact, and likely if the data genuinely favor it. I model each search as data plus noise from search idiosyncrasies and show that convergence across k searches screens off idiosyncrasy at a rate exponential in k. This gives philosophical foundations to 'multiverse analyses' (Steegen et al.) and specification-curve methods. It also shows that these methods partially restore the predictive advantage without new data, contrary to the assumption that only fresh data can.
why_new: Robustness analysis (Levins; Wimsatt; Weisberg) and predictivism have developed separately, and multiverse methods lack an epistemological rationale. The thesis connects them, and identifies a non-temporal route to predictive-grade evidence that both temporal and use-novelty accounts deem impossible.
